overview:
Leshya (leśyā) in Jainism is a technical doctrine within the broader theory of karma that describes the ‘coloring’ or ‘tonality’ of the soul due to its association with karmic matter. The term literally refers to the way the soul, which is intrinsically pure and luminous, appears tinged by the qualities of the karmic particles bound to it. Classical Jain texts explain this through the analogy of a crystal: just as a clear crystal appears colored when placed next to a colored object, the soul appears to take on the qualities of the karmic matter with which it is associated. This coloring is not merely visual but is described in terms of color, taste, smell, and touch, though in practice the six leshyas are usually referred to by their colors.

In the canonical Śvetāmbara text Uttarādhyayana-sūtra, chapter 34, a full statement of the theory of leshya is given. Six principal leshyas are enumerated: black (kṛṣṇa), blue (nīla), grey (kapota), red (tejo), yellow (padma), and white (śukla). These are divided into three ‘bad’ leshyas (black, blue, grey) and three ‘good’ leshyas (red, yellow, white). Each leshya is described with a set of analogies for its color—such as rain-clouds, buffalo horns, or conch shells—as well as its taste, smell, and tactile quality. The text further associates each leshya with particular mental dispositions and ethical tendencies: the darker leshyas correspond to states of cruelty, violence, deceit, and carelessness, while the lighter leshyas correspond to increasing degrees of self-control, compassion, and spiritual refinement.

Leshya is thus a way of classifying the moral and psychological condition of a living being at a given time. It is not a permanent label but a dynamic state that can change as one’s intentions, emotions, and actions change. Jain authors use vivid parables to illustrate this, most famously the ‘parable of the tree’, in which six travelers encounter a fruit-bearing tree and respond in different ways—from wanting to uproot the entire tree to gently plucking only ripe fruits. Each response is said to reflect a different leshya, showing how the same external situation can reveal very different inner dispositions. The doctrine emphasizes that karma is not only about physical acts but also about the subtle coloring of the soul by mental attitudes.

From a technical standpoint, leshya is closely linked to the Jain analysis of karma and the stages of spiritual development (guṇasthāna). The Uttarādhyayana-sūtra mentions degrees of leshya in geometric progressions (three, nine, twenty-seven, eighty-one, two hundred and forty-three), indicating a fine-grained gradation of psychic states. As a practitioner advances on the path—through right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct—the leshya becomes progressively purer, culminating in the white leshya associated with the highest spiritual condition. In the state of kevala-jñāna (omniscience) and ultimately liberation (mokṣa), the soul is completely free from karmic coloring and therefore beyond leshya.

Different Jain traditions—Digambara and Śvetāmbara—accept the basic framework of six leshyas, though they may differ in textual sources and interpretive emphasis. Later commentaries and cosmological manuals, such as the Śvetāmbara Saṃgrahaṇīratna, visually depict the six leshyas with colored diagrams and link them to broader cosmological and ethical teachings. Modern scholarship notes that the careful metrical structure of the Uttarādhyayana chapter on leshya suggests an early core of verses later expanded and systematized, showing how the doctrine was refined over time. In contemporary Jain teaching, leshya is often presented as a practical tool for self-reflection: by examining one’s reactions, intentions, and emotional tone, a layperson can gauge whether their current leshya tends toward the darker or lighter side and adjust their conduct accordingly.

Importantly, leshya is not a deterministic label that fixes a person’s worth; rather, it is a descriptive framework for understanding how karmic association manifests in lived experience. The doctrine underscores the Jain emphasis on inner transformation: changing one’s leshya—from black or blue toward red, yellow, and ultimately white—means cultivating non-violence, truthfulness, self-restraint, and detachment. While the imagery of colors and tastes is striking, traditional texts consistently tie leshya back to ethical practice and spiritual progress, reminding practitioners that the true goal is the complete purification of the soul beyond all coloring.

primary_sources.title: Uttarādhyayana-sūtra, Chapter 34 (On Leśyā)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Gaṇadhara Sudharma Svāmī; preserved in the Śvetāmbara canon
primary_sources.original_text:
इह लेस्सा-ओ वक्खामि, णिस्सइ सुनह जावणं। णामं वण्णं रसगंधं, फासं तं तं पमाणियं॥
कृष्णा नीला कपोत्ता, तेजा पद्मा सुक्कला।
कृष्णा लेस्सा मेघवण्णा, महिसस्स सिंगवण्णिया। रिस्टकफलवण्णा वा, खंजणअक्खिवण्णिया॥
सुक्कला लेस्सा संखवण्णा, अङ्कसिलावण्णिया। कुंदफुलवण्णा वा, धावंतदुधवण्णिया॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
iha lesyāo vakkhāmi, nissai sunaha jāvaṇaṃ. nāmaṃ vaṇṇaṃ rasagandhaṃ, phāsaṃ taṃ taṃ pamāṇiyaṃ.
kṛṣṇā nīlā kapottā, tejā padmā sukkalā.
kṛṣṇā lesyā meghavaṇṇā, mahisassa siṃgavaṇṇiyā. riṣṭakaphalavaṇṇā vā, khañjaṇakkhivaṇṇiyā.
sukkalā lesyā saṃkhavaṇṇā, aṅkasilāvaṇṇiyā. kundaphulavaṇṇā vā, dhāvantadudhavaṇṇiyā.
primary_sources.translation: “I shall expound here the leshyas; listen attentively to their nature: their names, colors, tastes, smells, touches, and their respective degrees. They are named in the following order: black, blue, grey, red, yellow, and white. The black leshya has the color of a rain-cloud, of a buffalo’s horn, of the fruit called riṣṭaka, or of the eye of the wagtail. The white leshya has the color of a conch-shell, of the aṅka-stone, of kunda flowers, of flowing milk.” (Translation adapted from Hermann Jacobi’s English rendering of the Uttarādhyayana-sūtra, with minor normalization.)
primary_sources.notes: This chapter is the principal canonical source for the doctrine of leshya in the Śvetāmbara tradition. It systematically lists the six leshyas, describing each in terms of color, taste, smell, touch, degrees, character, variety, duration, result, and associated lifespan. The verses quoted here illustrate the introductory framing and the color analogies for black and white leshyas. The full chapter continues with detailed descriptions of the mental dispositions corresponding to each leshya, distinguishing three ‘bad’ and three ‘good’ leshyas. The metrical structure—older śloka verses expanded by āryā verses—has been noted by modern scholars as evidence of editorial refinement over time.

primary_sources.title: Uttarādhyayana-sūtra, Parable of the Tree (within Chapter 34)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Gaṇadhara Sudharma Svāmī; Śvetāmbara canon
primary_sources.original_text:
एगं दंसरुक्खं दिट्ठुं, णहुत्ते छे जणाअ।
कृष्णलेस्सी उवउच्छेदं, नीलेस्सी छेदमिच्छइ।
कपोत्तलेस्सी फलं छेदं, तेजलेस्सी पत्तछेदं।
पद्मलेस्सी पक्कफलच्छेदं, सुक्कलेस्सी पक्कफलप्पहाणं॥
primary_sources.transliteration: egaṃ daṃsarukkhaṃ diṭṭhuṃ, nahutte che janā. kṛṣṇalesyī uvaucchedaṃ, nīlesyī chedamicchai. kapottalesyī phalaṃ chedaṃ, tejalesyī pattachedaṃ. padmalesyī pakkaphalachedaṃ, sukkalesyī pakkaphalappahāṇaṃ.
primary_sources.translation: “Six persons once saw a fruit-bearing tree. The man with black leshya wished to uproot it entirely. The man with blue leshya wished to cut down its trunk. The man with grey leshya wished to cut off its branches with the fruits. The man with red leshya wished to cut off only the leaves. The man with yellow leshya wished to cut off only the unripe fruits. The man with white leshya wished to take only the ripe fruits, leaving the tree standing.” (Translation synthesized from standard English renderings of the parable.)
primary_sources.notes: This famous parable illustrates how different leshyas correspond to different mental attitudes toward the same situation. The tree symbolizes a living being or a resource; the six responses range from total destruction to minimal, considerate use. The parable is widely cited in Jain teaching and visualized in illustrated manuscripts such as the Saṃgrahaṇīratna. It serves as a pedagogical tool for laypeople to reflect on their own tendencies and to cultivate the gentler, more restrained dispositions associated with the lighter leshyas.

primary_sources.title: Saṃgrahaṇīratna (Śvetāmbara cosmological manual)
primary_sources.author: Śrīcandra (Śvetāmbara author, c. 14th–15th century)
primary_sources.original_text:
कृष्णनीलकपोत्तेजो पद्मा सुक्कला लेस्सा णाम।
तेसिं वण्णरसगंधफासपमाणचरित्तफलजिवा॥
primary_sources.transliteration: kṛṣṇanīlakapottejo padmā sukkalā lesyā nāma. tesiṃ vaṇṇarasagandhaphāsapamāṇacarittaphalajīvā.
primary_sources.translation: “Black, blue, grey, red, yellow, and white are the leshyas by name. Their color, taste, smell, touch, degrees, character, fruits, and associated lives (are to be understood accordingly).” (Translation adapted from standard summaries of Saṃgrahaṇīratna passages on leshya.)
primary_sources.notes: Saṃgrahaṇīratna is a Śvetāmbara cosmological and doctrinal compendium that includes sections summarizing the leshya doctrine, often accompanied by colored diagrams in illustrated manuscripts. While not a primary canonical text, it functions as a traditional commentary and teaching aid (Corpus tier B–C). It reinforces the sixfold classification and connects leshya to broader cosmological and karmic structures.

misconceptions.myth: Leshya is simply a literal aura or physical color surrounding the body that can be seen by anyone.
misconceptions.reality: Classical Jain texts describe leshya as the ‘coloring’ of the soul due to karmic association, using color imagery as a symbolic and doctrinal tool. The six leshyas are linked to mental states, ethical dispositions, and karmic conditions, not to a universally visible physical halo. While some modern interpretations speak metaphorically of ‘auras’, the canonical sources emphasize inner attitudes and karmic qualities rather than externally observable colors.

misconceptions.myth: A person’s leshya is fixed for life and determines their fate in a rigid, unchangeable way.
misconceptions.reality: Leshya is a dynamic classification of the soul’s current karmic coloring and mental disposition. The Uttarādhyayana-sūtra and later Jain teaching present leshya as something that can change as one’s intentions, emotions, and actions change. Through right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct, a practitioner can move from darker leshyas toward lighter ones, gradually purifying the soul. The doctrine is meant to encourage ethical transformation, not to impose a fatalistic label.

misconceptions.myth: Only monks and nuns have leshya; laypeople are outside this doctrine.
misconceptions.reality: The doctrine of leshya applies to all embodied souls, including laypeople. The parable of the tree and many didactic explanations are explicitly aimed at lay audiences, inviting them to examine their reactions and cultivate gentler, more restrained attitudes. While ascetics are expected to attain purer leshyas through rigorous discipline, lay practitioners also engage with leshya as part of their ethical and spiritual self-assessment.

misconceptions.myth: The six leshyas correspond directly and exclusively to modern psychological personality types or clinical diagnoses.
misconceptions.reality: Leshya is a premodern Jain doctrinal framework rooted in karma theory and spiritual ethics. Although it speaks about mental states and dispositions, it does not map neatly onto modern psychological typologies or clinical categories. Using leshya to label oneself or others in medical or diagnostic terms goes beyond the intent and evidence of the traditional texts. For questions involving mental health or clinical assessment, qualified medical and psychological professionals should be consulted; leshya remains a spiritual-ethical concept.
